chapter: Ch 3 — Prospectus and Allotment of Securities

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 23 · Routes to issue securities
questions.stem: Under section 23 of the Companies Act 2013, which of the following routes is NOT available to a private company for the issue of its securities?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 23(2) read with s. 2(68)

readLink.label: Read: Two routes to raising securities — s. 23 →

options.text: A private placement under section 42
options.explanation: Expressly available to a private company under s. 23(2)(a).

options.text: A rights issue under section 62
options.explanation: Expressly available under s. 23(2)(b).

options.text: A bonus issue under section 62
options.explanation: Expressly available under s. 23(2)(b) along with a rights issue.

options.text: A public offer of securities through a prospectus
options.explanation: Correct. Section 23(2) gives a private company only private placement and rights or bonus issues. A public offer is confined to public companies by s. 23(1), and s. 2(68) requires a private company's articles to prohibit any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 42(3) proviso · No renunciation
questions.stem: An identified person who receives a private placement offer-cum-application letter wishes to renounce it in favour of his son. Which statement reflects the position under section 42?

readLink.label: Read: Private placement — s. 42 →

options.text: He may renounce it, provided the son is also recorded by the company as an identified person
options.explanation: Recording the son would make him a fresh identified person consuming the cap; it does not create a renunciation right, which the proviso denies outright.

options.text: He may not renounce it — the private placement offer and application carries no right of renunciation
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 42(3) states in terms that the private placement offer and application shall not carry any right of renunciation. The offer is personal to the identified person selected by the Board.

options.text: He may renounce it, because renunciation is a right attaching to every offer of securities by a company
options.explanation: Renunciation is characteristic of a rights issue under s. 62(1)(a)(ii), not of a private placement.

options.text: He may renounce it with the previous approval of the Registrar
options.explanation: The Registrar has no role in a private placement offer, and no approval can create a right the section removes.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 2(70) · Meaning of prospectus
questions.stem: A company circulates to the public a four-page document headed 'Investor Information Note — this is not a prospectus', which describes its forthcoming debenture issue and invites readers to apply. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: What counts as a prospectus →

options.text: It is a prospectus, because section 2(70) catches any notice, circular, advertisement or other document inviting offers from the public for the subscription or purchase of securities
options.explanation: Correct. The definition looks at substance, not at the label. A document that invites offers from the public for securities is a prospectus however it describes itself, and the disclaimer changes nothing.

options.text: It is not a prospectus, because it expressly disclaims that character
options.explanation: The label is irrelevant. If a disclaimer were enough, s. 2(70) could be defeated by a line of print.

options.text: It is not a prospectus, because a prospectus must be a document issued only for equity shares
options.explanation: 'Securities' includes debentures; s. 2(70) is not confined to shares.

options.text: It is a prospectus only if the company is a listed company
options.explanation: Listing is irrelevant to s. 2(70). The definition applies to any body corporate inviting offers from the public.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 33 · Abridged prospectus
questions.stem: Under section 33(1) of the Companies Act 2013, no application form for the purchase of any securities of a company shall be issued unless it is accompanied by:

readLink.label: Read: Abridged prospectus — s. 33 →

options.text: A copy of the memorandum and articles of the company
options.explanation: Copies of the memorandum and articles are supplied to members under s. 17 on request; they have nothing to do with the application form.

options.text: A certified copy of the resolution authorising the issue
options.explanation: The authority for the issue and the resolution details are stated in the prospectus under s. 26(1), but the resolution itself need not accompany the form.

options.text: An abridged prospectus
options.explanation: Correct. Section 33(1) requires an abridged prospectus — the memorandum containing the salient features of a prospectus specified by SEBI (s. 2(1)) — to accompany every application form, so the investor sees the essentials at the moment of decision.

options.text: The auditor's report on the profits and losses of the company for the last five financial years
options.explanation: The auditor's report is content of the prospectus under s. 26(1); it is not a separate attachment to the application form.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 33 · Exceptions and penalty
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about section 33 is INCORRECT?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 33(1) proviso, s. 33(2) and s. 33(3)

readLink.label: Read: Abridged prospectus — s. 33 →

options.text: No abridged prospectus is required where the offer is made in connection with a bona fide invitation to a person to enter into an underwriting agreement
options.explanation: This is the first limb of the proviso to s. 33(1) and is correctly stated.

options.text: A copy of the full prospectus need not be furnished to an applicant in any circumstances once an abridged prospectus has been supplied
options.explanation: Correct. This is the incorrect statement, and therefore the answer. Section 33(2) requires a copy of the full prospectus to be furnished to any person, before the closing of the subscription list and the offer, on his request.

options.text: No abridged prospectus is required where the securities are not offered to the public
options.explanation: This is the second limb of the proviso to s. 33(1) and is correctly stated — which is why a private placement under s. 42 needs no abridged prospectus.

options.text: A company issuing an application form in contravention of section 33 is liable to a penalty of ₹50,000 for each default
options.explanation: Section 33(3) fixes the penalty at ₹50,000 for each default; the statement is correct.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 31 · Shelf prospectus
questions.stem: Regarding a shelf prospectus under section 31, which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Shelf prospectus — s. 31 →

options.text: Any company may file a shelf prospectus, and it is valid for one year from the date of filing with the Registrar
options.explanation: Two errors. Only a class of companies provided by SEBI regulations may file one, and the validity runs from the opening of the first offer, not from filing.

options.text: Any company may file a shelf prospectus, and it is valid for two years from the date of opening of the first offer
options.explanation: The eligibility is restricted to a SEBI-prescribed class, and the maximum validity is one year, not two.

options.text: Only a class of companies prescribed by SEBI may file one, and it is valid for one year from the date of filing with the Registrar
options.explanation: The eligibility limb is right but the clock is wrong: validity runs from the date of opening of the first offer of securities under the shelf prospectus.

options.text: Only a class of companies provided by SEBI regulations may file one at the stage of the first offer, and it must indicate a period of validity not exceeding one year commencing from the date of opening of the first offer
options.explanation: Correct. Section 31(1) restricts the facility to a SEBI-prescribed class, requires filing at the stage of the first offer, and fixes the maximum validity at one year running from the opening of the first offer — after which no further prospectus is needed for offers within the period.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 31(2) proviso · Withdrawal by applicants
questions.stem: A company that has filed a shelf prospectus receives applications with advance payment for a second tranche. Before the information memorandum notes a change in the company's financial position, one applicant is intimated of the change and wishes to withdraw. Under the proviso to section 31(2), the company must:

readLink.label: Read: Shelf prospectus — s. 31 →

options.text: Refund the whole of the money received from him as advance payment
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 31(2) requires the company to intimate the changes to applicants who paid in advance and, where any of them wishes to withdraw, to refund the whole of the money received as advance payment, within the prescribed time and manner.

options.text: Refund the advance payment after deducting the proportionate issue expenses
options.explanation: There is no deduction. The proviso speaks of refunding the whole of the money received as advance payment.

options.text: Retain the money and allot securities, the applicant having no right to withdraw once advance payment is made
options.explanation: The whole purpose of the proviso is to give an exit to a person who committed on information that has since changed.

options.text: Refund the money only if the change relates to a new charge created on the company's assets
options.explanation: The proviso is not confined to new charges; s. 31(2) covers new charges, changes in financial position and other prescribed matters alike.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 32 · Red herring prospectus
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a red herring prospectus under section 32?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, Explanation to s. 32 and s. 32(3)

readLink.label: Read: Red herring prospectus — s. 32 →

options.text: A prospectus issued after the closing of the offer, stating the final price at which the securities were allotted
options.explanation: That describes the final prospectus filed under s. 32(4) after the offer closes, not the red herring prospectus that precedes it.

options.text: A prospectus which does not include complete particulars of the quantum or price of the securities included in it, and which carries the same obligations as a prospectus
options.explanation: Correct. The Explanation to s. 32 defines it by the missing quantum or price, and s. 32(3) makes it carry the same obligations as a prospectus — so ss. 34 and 35 apply to it in full.

options.text: A prospectus which contains no financial information, issued only to qualified institutional buyers
options.explanation: A red herring prospectus contains the full s. 26 disclosure except the quantum or price, and it is a public-offer document, not a QIB-only one.

options.text: A prospectus filed by a class of companies prescribed by SEBI, valid for one year from the opening of the first offer
options.explanation: That is a shelf prospectus under s. 31.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 32(2) · Filing of the red herring prospectus
questions.stem: A red herring prospectus must be filed with the Registrar:

readLink.label: Read: Red herring prospectus — s. 32 →

options.text: At least thirty days before the opening of the subscription list and the offer
options.explanation: Thirty days is the s. 39(3) minimum-subscription window; it has nothing to do with the filing of a red herring prospectus.

options.text: At least seven days before the opening of the subscription list and the offer
options.explanation: Seven days is not the period. Section 32(2) fixes three days.

options.text: Within three days after the closing of the subscription list and the offer
options.explanation: The filing is before the opening, not after the closing. What follows the closing is the final prospectus under s. 32(4).

options.text: At least three days prior to the opening of the subscription list and the offer
options.explanation: Correct. Section 32(2) requires filing with the Registrar at least three days before the opening of the subscription list and the offer.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 32(4) · Filing after the offer closes
questions.stem: Upon the closing of an offer made through a red herring prospectus, the prospectus stating the total capital raised (by way of debt or share capital), the closing price of the securities and other details not included in the red herring prospectus must be filed with:

readLink.label: Read: Red herring prospectus — s. 32 →

options.text: The Registrar and the Securities and Exchange Board of India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 32(4) names both — the Registrar and SEBI. Answering 'the Registrar' alone is the most common slip in this area.

options.text: The Registrar alone
options.explanation: Incomplete. Section 32(4) requires filing with SEBI as well.

options.text: The Securities and Exchange Board of India alone
options.explanation: Incomplete in the other direction; the Registrar is also named.

options.text: The Registrar, the Securities and Exchange Board of India and the recognised stock exchange concerned
options.explanation: The stock exchange is not named in s. 32(4). Its role in a public offer arises under s. 40(1) — obtaining permission for the securities to be dealt with.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 25(2) · Deemed prospectus presumption
questions.stem: Under section 25(2), it is evidence that an allotment of securities was made with a view to their being offered for sale to the public if it is shown that:

readLink.label: Read: Deemed prospectus and offer for sale — ss. 25 and 28 →

options.text: The offer for sale to the public was made within twelve months after the allotment or agreement to allot
options.explanation: The period in s. 25(2)(a) is six months, not twelve.

options.text: The offer for sale to the public was made within six months after the allotment, and the whole consideration had not been received by the company at the date of the offer
options.explanation: The two limbs of s. 25(2) are alternatives joined by 'or'. Requiring both to be satisfied states the test too narrowly.

options.text: The offer for sale to the public was made within six months after the allotment or agreement to allot, or that at the date when the offer was made the whole consideration to be received by the company had not been so received
options.explanation: Correct. Section 25(2) offers two independent evidentiary limbs — the six-month proximity in clause (a), or the unpaid consideration in clause (b). Either alone is enough.

options.text: The allottee was a body corporate engaged in the business of dealing in securities
options.explanation: The identity or business of the allottee is not the statutory test; s. 25(2) turns on timing or unpaid consideration.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 42 Explanation III · Deemed public offer
questions.stem: An unlisted company allots securities to more than the prescribed number of persons in a financial year under what it describes as a private placement. Under Explanation III to section 42, the consequence is that:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, Explanation III to s. 42

readLink.label: Read: Private placement — s. 42 →

options.text: The allotment beyond the prescribed number is void, and only those allotments are set aside
options.explanation: Explanation III does not void the excess allotments; it re-characterises the whole offer as a public offer.

options.text: The offer is deemed to be an offer to the public and is governed by Part I of Chapter III, whether or not payment has been received and whether or not the company intends to list the securities
options.explanation: Correct. Explanation III applies to listed and unlisted companies alike and expressly disregards both whether the payment has been received and whether the company intends to list anywhere in or outside India. The company is treated as having made a public offer — without a prospectus.

options.text: The consequence follows only if the company has actually received the subscription money
options.explanation: Explanation III applies 'whether the payment for the securities has been received or not'.

options.text: The consequence follows only if the company intends to list the securities on a recognised stock exchange
options.explanation: Explanation III applies whether or not the company intends to list its securities in or outside India.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 28 · Offer for sale by members
questions.stem: Certain members of a company, in consultation with the Board, offer part of their holding of shares to the public under section 28. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Deemed prospectus and offer for sale — ss. 25 and 28 →

options.text: The document by which the offer is made is a prospectus issued by the offering members personally, and the company bears no responsibility for it
options.explanation: Section 28(2) deems it a prospectus issued by the company, so the company and its officers are drawn in.

options.text: The company must bear the expenses of the offer, since the document is deemed to be its own prospectus
options.explanation: The opposite: s. 28(3) requires the members to reimburse the company all expenses incurred by it on the offer.

options.text: No prospectus law applies at all, because no fresh securities are being issued by the company
options.explanation: Section 2(70) covers an invitation for the purchase of securities, and s. 28(2) applies all laws relating to a prospectus to the document.

options.text: The document is deemed to be a prospectus issued by the company, all laws relating to a prospectus apply to it, and the members must reimburse the company all expenses incurred by it on the offer
options.explanation: Correct. Section 28(2) supplies the deeming and the application of prospectus law; s. 28(3) puts the cost back on the selling members, who are the ones taking the money.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 26(1) · Matters to be stated
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT among the matters section 26(1) requires a prospectus to state?

readLink.label: Read: Matters to be stated and registration — s. 26 →

options.text: The names and addresses of every member holding more than five per cent of the paid-up share capital of the company
options.explanation: Correct. This is the item not required, and therefore the answer. Section 26(1) calls for the names and addresses of the company secretary, chief financial officer, auditors, bankers, trustees for debenture holders, underwriters and such other persons as may be prescribed; a five per cent shareholder list is not part of that catalogue.

options.text: A statement by the Board that all monies received out of the issue shall be transferred to a separate bank account as mentioned in section 40(3)
options.explanation: Expressly required by s. 26(1); it is the disclosure counterpart of the s. 40(3) obligation.

options.text: Particulars of any litigation or legal action pending or taken by a Government Department or a statutory body during the last five years immediately preceding the issue against the promoter of the company
options.explanation: Expressly required by s. 26(1) — and the five-year period is itself examinable.

options.text: The minimum subscription, the premium payable on securities and the procedure and time schedule for allotment and issue of securities
options.explanation: All three are expressly required by s. 26(1).

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 26(3) · Expert's consent
questions.stem: A prospectus is to include a valuation report. Which statement correctly states the section 26(3) requirement and the meaning of 'expert' for this purpose?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 26(3) and the Explanation thereto

readLink.label: Read: Matters to be stated and registration — s. 26 →

options.text: Oral consent of the expert suffices, provided the prospectus records that consent was obtained
options.explanation: Section 26(3) requires written consent; recording an oral consent does not satisfy it.

options.text: The expert may be a person who has been engaged in the promotion of the company, so long as the engagement is disclosed
options.explanation: The Explanation to s. 26(3) disqualifies such a person outright; disclosure does not cure it.

options.text: The expert must have given his written consent to the issue and not withdrawn it before delivery of a copy of the prospectus to the Registrar, the prospectus must say so, and he must not be and not have been engaged or interested in the formation, promotion or management of the company
options.explanation: Correct. Section 26(3) combines three requirements — written consent, consent still standing at the date of delivery to the Registrar, and a statement in the prospectus to that effect — while the Explanation confines 'expert' to an independent person.

options.text: The expert's consent must be obtained at any time before the closing of the subscription list
options.explanation: The consent must not have been withdrawn before delivery of a copy to the Registrar — a much earlier point than the closing of the subscription list.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 26(8) · Ninety-day validity
questions.stem: Section 26(8) provides that a prospectus shall not be valid if it is issued more than ninety days after a certain date. That date is the date on which:

readLink.label: Read: Matters to be stated and registration — s. 26 →

options.text: The Board of Directors approves the prospectus
options.explanation: Board approval is an internal step and starts no statutory clock.

options.text: A copy of the prospectus is delivered to the Registrar for registration
options.explanation: Correct. Section 26(8) runs the ninety days from the date on which a copy is delivered to the Registrar under s. 26(4), so a prospectus held back too long after delivery lapses and must be re-delivered.

options.text: The Registrar registers the prospectus
options.explanation: Registration is the Registrar's act and may follow delivery by some days; the clock is fixed to delivery, and this is the most attractive wrong answer.

options.text: The subscription list opens
options.explanation: The opening of the subscription list is the event the prospectus is issued for; it cannot also be the start of the validity period.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 27 · Variation of terms or objects
questions.stem: A company that raised money through a prospectus proposes to vary the objects for which the prospectus was issued. Under section 27(1) it must:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 27(1) and its provisos

readLink.label: Read: Variation of terms or objects — s. 27 →

options.text: Pass a Board resolution and file it with the Registrar within thirty days
options.explanation: The Board cannot authorise the variation. Section 27(1) reserves it to the members.

options.text: Pass an ordinary resolution and publish the notice on the company's website
options.explanation: An ordinary resolution is insufficient, and the publicity requirement is wider than the website alone.

options.text: Obtain the previous approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: Central Government approval belongs to a change of name (s. 13(2)) and a State-to-State shift of the registered office (s. 13(4)); it has no role under s. 27.

options.text: Obtain the approval of, or an authority given by, the company in general meeting by way of a special resolution, and publish the details of the notice in two newspapers — one English and one in the vernacular language of the city where the registered office is situated — and on its website, indicating the justification for the variation
options.explanation: Correct. Section 27(1) requires the members' special resolution, and the first proviso requires the twin-newspaper and website publication with the justification stated.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 27(2) · Dissenting shareholders' exit
questions.stem: Where the terms of a contract referred to in the prospectus or the objects for which it was issued are varied, section 27(2) requires that dissenting shareholders be given an exit offer. That exit offer is to be given by:

readLink.label: Read: Variation of terms or objects — s. 27 →

options.text: The promoters or controlling shareholders, at such exit price and in such manner and conditions as may be specified by SEBI by regulations
options.explanation: Correct. Section 27(2) puts the burden on the promoters or controlling shareholders — those who wanted the change — and leaves the exit price and mechanics to SEBI regulations.

options.text: The company itself, by way of a buy-back under section 68
options.explanation: Section 27(2) does not route the exit through a buy-back, and the company is not the offeror.

options.text: The underwriters to the issue, in proportion to the securities underwritten by them
options.explanation: Underwriters have no obligation of this kind; their role ends with the subscription commitment under s. 40(6).

options.text: The Central Government, out of the Investor Education and Protection Fund
options.explanation: The IEPF receives disgorged amounts under s. 38(4) and unclaimed sums; it does not fund shareholder exits.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 29 · Issue in dematerialised form
questions.stem: Under section 29 of the Companies Act 2013, which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Demat issue and advertisement — ss. 29 and 30 →

options.text: Every company, without exception, must issue and hold all its securities only in dematerialised form
options.explanation: Too wide. Section 29(2) leaves companies outside the mandatory classes free to issue in physical form under the Act or in dematerialised form under the Depositories Act.

options.text: Only listed companies are required to issue securities in dematerialised form
options.explanation: The trigger in s. 29(1) is the making of a public offer, not listing, and prescribed classes are covered too.

options.text: Every company making a public offer, and such other class of companies as may be prescribed, must issue securities only in dematerialised form by complying with the Depositories Act 1996; prescribed classes of unlisted companies must also hold and transfer securities only in that form
options.explanation: Correct. Section 29(1) fixes the issue obligation on public offers and prescribed classes, and s. 29(1A) extends holding and transfer to prescribed classes of unlisted companies.

options.text: A company may convert its securities into dematerialised form only with the previous approval of the Registrar
options.explanation: Section 29(2) permits conversion without any such approval; the machinery is the Depositories Act, not a Registrar's consent.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 30 · Advertisement of prospectus
questions.stem: Where an advertisement of a company's prospectus is published, section 30 requires the advertisement to specify:

readLink.label: Read: Demat issue and advertisement — ss. 29 and 30 →

options.text: Only the name of the company, the amount of the issue and the dates of opening and closing
options.explanation: Far too little. Section 30 requires the memorandum's substance to travel with the advertisement.

options.text: The contents of the memorandum as regards the objects, the liability of members and the amount of share capital of the company, the names of the signatories to the memorandum and the number of shares subscribed for by them, and the capital structure of the company
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30 lists exactly these, so that a short advertisement cannot bypass the disclosure the memorandum would otherwise force.

options.text: The full text of the auditor's report on the profits and losses of the company for the preceding five financial years
options.explanation: The auditor's reports are content of the prospectus under s. 26(1); s. 30 does not require them in the advertisement.

options.text: The names of the underwriters and the rate of commission payable to each of them
options.explanation: That disclosure belongs to the prospectus under the rules made for s. 40(6), not to the advertisement under s. 30.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 34 · Criminal liability for misstatements
questions.stem: A prospectus includes a statement which is untrue in the context in which it is included. Under section 34, liability attaches to:

readLink.label: Read: Criminal liability for misstatements — s. 34 →

options.text: The company alone, which is liable to pay compensation to every subscriber who suffered loss
options.explanation: Compensation to subscribers is s. 35 (civil liability). Section 34 is a criminal provision and does not fasten on the company alone.

options.text: Every subscriber who acted on the statement and sustained loss
options.explanation: A subscriber who acted on the statement is the claimant under s. 35, not a person liable.

options.text: Every director of the company, whether or not he authorised the issue of the prospectus
options.explanation: Section 34 fastens on the act of authorising the issue, not on the office of director as such.

options.text: Every person who authorises the issue of such prospectus, who is liable for action under section 447
options.explanation: Correct. Section 34 makes every person who authorises the issue of a prospectus containing an untrue or misleading statement — or a misleading inclusion or omission — liable under s. 447, without any need to prove that a particular investor relied on it.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 34 proviso · The defence
questions.stem: A director authorised the issue of a prospectus believing a forecast in it to be true, but learned two weeks before the prospectus was issued that the forecast was materially false and did nothing. On his defence under the proviso to section 34:

readLink.label: Read: Criminal liability for misstatements — s. 34 →

options.text: The defence fails, because the proviso requires that he had reasonable grounds to believe and did believe the statement to be true up to the time of the issue of the prospectus
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso protects only a belief that survives to the moment of issue. A belief abandoned two weeks earlier is no defence, and the statement is admittedly material, so the other limb of the proviso is unavailable too.

options.text: The defence succeeds, because he honestly believed the statement when he authorised the issue
options.explanation: Belief at the time of authorisation is not the statutory test; the proviso fixes the moment of issue.

options.text: The defence succeeds, because the proviso protects any person who did not personally draft the statement
options.explanation: The proviso says nothing about who drafted the statement.

options.text: The defence succeeds if he can show that at least one other director also believed the statement
options.explanation: The defence is personal and turns on his own reasonable and actual belief, not on what colleagues believed.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 35(1) · Who is liable to compensate
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a category of person made liable to pay compensation under section 35(1)?

readLink.label: Read: Civil liability for misstatements — s. 35 →

options.text: A person who is a director of the company at the time of the issue of the prospectus
options.explanation: Expressly liable under s. 35(1)(a).

options.text: A promoter of the company
options.explanation: Expressly liable under s. 35(1)(c).

options.text: The registered owner of more than ten per cent of the paid-up share capital of the company
options.explanation: Correct. This is the category not named, and therefore the answer. Section 35(1) lists the company, directors at the time of issue, persons named as directors or as having agreed to become directors, promoters, persons who authorised the issue, and the expert. Shareholding as such creates no liability.

options.text: A person who has authorised himself to be named and is named in the prospectus as having agreed to become a director after an interval of time
options.explanation: Expressly liable under s. 35(1)(b).

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 35(2) · Defences to civil liability
questions.stem: Which of the following is a defence expressly available under section 35(2) to a person otherwise liable under section 35(1)?

readLink.label: Read: Civil liability for misstatements — s. 35 →

options.text: That he relied on information supplied by the company's auditors and had no reason to doubt it
options.explanation: Reliance on the auditors is not one of the two defences in s. 35(2).

options.text: That the prospectus was issued without his knowledge or consent and that, on becoming aware of its issue, he forthwith gave a reasonable public notice to that effect
options.explanation: Correct. This is s. 35(2)(b) exactly — and note both halves: absence of knowledge or consent, plus a reasonable public notice given forthwith on learning of the issue. Silence destroys the defence.

options.text: That the misleading statement was made by an expert whose consent had been obtained
options.explanation: The expert's own liability under s. 35(1)(e) does not excuse the others.

options.text: That the subscriber had an opportunity to inspect the company's audited accounts before subscribing
options.explanation: The subscriber's opportunity to investigate is not a statutory defence under s. 35(2).

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 35(3) · Prospectus issued to defraud
questions.stem: Where it is proved that a prospectus has been issued with intent to defraud the applicants for the securities or for any fraudulent purpose, section 35(3) provides that every person referred to in section 35(1) shall be:

readLink.label: Read: Civil liability for misstatements — s. 35 →

options.text: Liable only to the extent of the amount he personally received out of the issue
options.explanation: Section 35(3) contains no such measure; it removes the limitation on liability rather than creating one.

options.text: Liable to compensate only those subscribers who applied after the fraud came to light
options.explanation: The sub-section covers any person who subscribed on the basis of the prospectus.

options.text: Relieved of liability if he proves he took reasonable care, the fraud being that of the company
options.explanation: Fraud widens liability under s. 35(3); it does not open a care-based escape.

options.text: Personally responsible, without any limitation of liability, for all or any of the losses or damages incurred by any person who subscribed to the securities on the basis of that prospectus
options.explanation: Correct. Section 35(3) strips the ceiling: proof of fraudulent intent makes every s. 35(1) person personally responsible without any limitation of liability.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 36 · Fraudulently inducing investment
questions.stem: Which statement about section 36 of the Companies Act 2013 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Fraudulent inducement, impersonation and class action →

options.text: It requires no prospectus at all, and extends to statements, promises or forecasts made to induce a person to enter into an agreement with a view to obtaining credit facilities from any bank or financial institution
options.explanation: Correct. Section 36 is not tied to any document: any person who knowingly or recklessly makes a false, deceptive or misleading statement, promise or forecast, or deliberately conceals material facts, to induce another into a securities agreement, a yield-or-fluctuation agreement, or an agreement with a view to obtaining bank or financial-institution credit, is liable under s. 447.

options.text: It applies only where the false statement appears in a registered prospectus
options.explanation: That is the domain of ss. 34 and 35. Section 36 needs no prospectus.

options.text: It applies only to statements made by a director or promoter of the company
options.explanation: Section 36 opens with 'any person'; it is not confined to insiders.

options.text: It applies only where the statement is made knowingly, so a recklessly made statement falls outside it
options.explanation: The section says 'knowingly or recklessly'. Recklessness is expressly caught.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 38 · Personation for acquisition of securities
questions.stem: A person makes eleven applications for shares of a company in different combinations of his name and surname. On conviction under section 38, which additional order may the Court pass, and where does the amount go?

readLink.label: Read: Fraudulent inducement, impersonation and class action →

options.text: An order directing the company to cancel the allotment, the amount being refunded to the applicant
options.explanation: Section 38(3) is not a refund provision; the wrongdoer does not get his money back as of right, and cancellation is not the named remedy.

options.text: An order of disgorgement of the gain, the amount being credited to the general revenues of the Central Government
options.explanation: The disgorgement limb is right but the destination is wrong — s. 38(4) names the Investor Education and Protection Fund.

options.text: An order for disgorgement of the gain made and for seizure and disposal of the securities in his possession, the amount received being credited to the Investor Education and Protection Fund
options.explanation: Correct. Section 38(3) empowers the Court, on conviction, to order disgorgement of the gain and the seizure and disposal of the securities held; s. 38(4) credits the proceeds to the Investor Education and Protection Fund.

options.text: An order restraining the company from making any further public offer for three years
options.explanation: Section 38 punishes the applicant, not the company; no such bar on the company exists in the section.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 39(1) · Minimum subscription
questions.stem: Securities have been offered to the public for subscription. The prospectus states a minimum amount, and applications have been received for only part of it. Under section 39(1):

readLink.label: Read: Allotment of securities — s. 39 →

options.text: The Board may allot to the extent of the applications received, provided it discloses the shortfall to the Registrar
options.explanation: There is no such discretion and no such disclosure route. The bar in s. 39(1) is absolute.

options.text: No allotment may be made unless the amount stated in the prospectus as the minimum amount has been subscribed and the sums payable on application for that amount have been paid to and received by the company
options.explanation: Correct. Section 39(1) imposes two cumulative conditions — the minimum amount subscribed, and the application sums for that amount actually received by cheque or other instrument. Until both are met the company cannot allot at all.

options.text: Allotment may be made if the underwriters undertake in writing to make good the shortfall at a later date
options.explanation: An undertaking is not receipt. Section 39(1) requires the sums to have been paid to and received by the company.

options.text: Allotment may be made with the approval of the members by special resolution
options.explanation: The members cannot waive s. 39(1); it exists to protect applicants, not the company.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 39(2) · Minimum application money
questions.stem: Sindhu Alloys Limited makes a public offer of 25,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹40 per share. SEBI has specified no higher percentage or amount. The minimum amount payable on application on the whole issue under section 39(2) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 39(2) — five per cent of the nominal amount

readLink.label: Read: Allotment of securities — s. 39 →

options.explanation: This applies 5% to the issue price of ₹50. Section 39(2) measures the floor against the NOMINAL amount of ₹10, not the price.
This is 10% of the nominal amount. The statutory floor is five per cent.
This is 2.5% of the nominal amount — the underwriting-commission rate for debentures, borrowed into the wrong provision.
Correct. 5% of the nominal amount = 5% × ₹10 = ₹0.50 per share; ₹0.50 × 25,00,000 shares = ₹12,50,000. The premium is irrelevant to the section 39(2) floor.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 39(3) · Thirty-day window
questions.stem: Aravalli Speciality Steels Limited issues its prospectus on 4 June 2026. SEBI has specified no other period. The last date by which the stated minimum amount must be subscribed and the sums payable on application received, failing which the money must be returned, is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 39(3) — thirty days from the date of issue of the prospectus

readLink.label: Read: Allotment of securities — s. 39 →

options.text: 4 July 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from 4 June 2026: 26 days take the count to 30 June, and 4 more to 4 July 2026. The clock in s. 39(3) runs from the date of issue of the prospectus.

options.text: 3 July 2026
options.explanation: One day short — the trigger day is excluded and day 1 is 5 June, so day 30 is 4 July.

options.text: 19 July 2026
options.explanation: This is 45 days. Section 39(3) allows thirty days, or such other period as SEBI may specify; none was specified here.

options.text: 2 September 2026
options.explanation: This is 90 days — the s. 26(8) validity period for the prospectus itself, not the s. 39(3) subscription window.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 39(4) · Return of allotment
questions.stem: Netravati Foods Limited, a company having a share capital, makes an allotment of equity shares on 14 September 2026 following a public offer. Under section 39(4) read with the prescribed rules, the return of allotment must be filed with the Registrar on or before:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 39(4) read with the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules 2014 — thirty days from allotment (rules-level)

readLink.label: Read: Allotment of securities — s. 39 →

options.text: 29 September 2026
options.explanation: This is 15 days — the period for a return of allotment on a PRIVATE PLACEMENT under s. 42(8), not for a public allotment.

options.text: 13 October 2026
options.explanation: One day short. Day 1 is 15 September, so day 30 is 14 October.

options.text: 14 October 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from 14 September 2026: 16 days take the count to 30 September, and 14 more to 14 October 2026.

options.text: 13 November 2026
options.explanation: This is 60 days — the s. 42(6) allotment window, borrowed into the wrong provision.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 41 · Global depository receipts
questions.stem: Under section 41 of the Companies Act 2013, a company may issue depository receipts in any foreign country:

readLink.label: Read: Global depository receipts — s. 41 →

options.text: By a resolution of its Board of Directors, in the prescribed manner and subject to the prescribed conditions
options.explanation: The Board cannot authorise it. Section 41 requires the members to act.

options.text: After passing a special resolution in its general meeting, in such manner and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed
options.explanation: Correct. Section 41 is a single sentence: a special resolution of the members, then issue in the prescribed manner on the prescribed conditions. The machinery is rules-level.

options.text: After passing an ordinary resolution and obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: Neither limb is right — the resolution must be special and no Central Government approval is required by the section.

options.text: With the previous approval of the Registrar of Companies within whose jurisdiction its registered office is situated
options.explanation: The Registrar has no approval role under s. 41.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 40 · Listing and application money
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about section 40 is INCORRECT?

readLink.label: Read: Listing, application money and commission — s. 40 →

options.text: Every company making a public offer must, before making the offer, apply to one or more recognised stock exchanges and obtain permission for its securities to be dealt with in them
options.explanation: This states s. 40(1) correctly, including that the application precedes the offer.

options.text: All monies received on application from the public for subscription must be kept in a separate bank account in a scheduled bank
options.explanation: This states s. 40(3) correctly.

options.text: The monies in that separate account may be used for adjustment against allotment where the securities have been permitted to be dealt with in the stock exchange, or for repayment where the company is for any other reason unable to allot securities
options.explanation: These are the only two permitted uses under s. 40(3)(a) and (b); the statement is correct.

options.text: An applicant may, by a term in the application form, validly agree to waive compliance with the requirements of section 40
options.explanation: Correct. This is the incorrect statement, and therefore the answer. Section 40(4) makes any condition purporting to require or bind an applicant to waive compliance with any requirement of the section VOID. The protection cannot be contracted away.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 40(6) · Underwriting commission on shares
questions.stem: Chandrabhaga Ports Limited makes a public offer of 50,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹40 per share. Its articles authorise the payment of underwriting commission at 6%. The maximum commission the company may pay on these shares under section 40(6) and the rules made thereunder is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 40(6) read with r. 13, Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules 2014 — 5% of the issue price or the rate in the articles, whichever is less (rules-level)

readLink.label: Read: Listing, application money and commission — s. 40 →

options.explanation: Correct. Issue value = ₹40 × 50,00,000 = ₹20,00,00,000. The rule caps commission on shares at 5% of the price at which the shares are issued = ₹1,00,00,000, and the articles' 6% (₹1,20,00,000) is higher, so the lower figure governs.
This is the articles' 6%. A generous article cannot raise the ceiling — the rule fixes the maximum and the articles can only reduce it.
This applies 5% to the face value of ₹10. The commission base is the PRICE at which the shares are issued, unlike the s. 39(2) floor, whose base is the nominal amount.
This applies 2.5% — the debenture cap — to the share issue.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 40(6) · Underwriting commission on debentures
questions.stem: The same company also offers 2,00,000 debentures of ₹100 each at par, its articles authorising underwriting commission at 4%. The maximum commission payable on the debentures is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 40(6) read with r. 13, Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules 2014 — 2.5% of the issue price or the rate in the articles, whichever is less (rules-level)

readLink.label: Read: Listing, application money and commission — s. 40 →

options.explanation: This is the articles' 4%. The rule caps debenture commission at 2.5% of the issue price, and the lower of the two governs.
This is 1.25% — half the correct rate.
Correct. Issue value = ₹100 × 2,00,000 = ₹2,00,00,000. The debenture cap is 2.5% of the price at which the debentures are issued = ₹5,00,000, which is lower than the articles' 4% (₹8,00,000).
This applies 5% — the cap for shares — to a debenture issue.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 42(2) · The 200-person cap
questions.stem: During the financial year 2026-27 Konkan Marine Foods Private Limited has already offered equity shares by private placement to 88 identified persons. In the same year it has separately offered securities to 30 qualified institutional buyers and to 45 employees under a scheme of employees' stock option. Assuming the prescribed maximum of 200 persons applies, the number of further identified persons to whom equity shares may still be offered in that financial year is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(2) read with r. 14, Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules 2014 — 200 persons per financial year, excluding QIBs and ESOP employees (rules-level)

readLink.label: Read: Private placement — s. 42 →

options.explanation: This counts the 30 qualified institutional buyers against the cap. QIBs are expressly excluded.
Correct. 200 − 88 = 112. Qualified institutional buyers and employees offered securities under an ESOP scheme are excluded from the count, so neither the 30 nor the 45 consumes any headroom.
This counts the 45 ESOP employees against the cap. They are expressly excluded.
This counts both the QIBs and the ESOP employees against the cap; both exclusions have been ignored.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 42(6) · Sixty-day allotment window
questions.stem: Under a private placement, Malaprabha Textiles Private Limited receives the application money from its identified persons on 12 May 2026. The last date by which it must allot the securities under section 42(6) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(6) — sixty days from the date of receipt of the application money

readLink.label: Read: Private placement — s. 42 →

options.text: 26 July 2026
options.explanation: This is the outer date for REPAYMENT — sixty days plus the further fifteen days — not the date for allotment.

options.text: 12 July 2026
options.explanation: One day too many; the trigger day is excluded, so day 1 is 13 May and day 60 is 11 July.

options.text: 10 August 2026
options.explanation: This is 90 days, which is the s. 26(8) prospectus-validity period and has no application to a private placement.

options.text: 11 July 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Sixty days from 12 May 2026: 19 days take the count to 31 May, 30 more to 30 June (day 49), and 11 more to 11 July 2026. The clock runs from the date of receipt of the application money.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 42(6) · Refund window
questions.stem: Under a private placement, Betwa Agro Industries Private Limited receives the application money on 18 August 2026 and makes no allotment at all. The last date by which it must repay the application money to the subscribers, before interest begins to be payable, is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(6) — repayment within fifteen days from the expiry of the sixty days

readLink.label: Read: Private placement — s. 42 →

options.text: 1 November 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Sixty days from 18 August 2026 expire on 17 October 2026 (13 days to 31 August, 30 to 30 September, 17 to 17 October). Fifteen days from that expiry gives 1 November 2026.

options.text: 17 October 2026
options.explanation: This is the last date to ALLOT. The repayment window is a further fifteen days beyond it.

options.text: 2 November 2026
options.explanation: One day too many — day 1 of the fifteen-day window is 18 October, so day 15 is 1 November.

options.text: 16 November 2026
options.explanation: This allows thirty days after the sixty, not fifteen. Thirty days is the s. 42(10) refund period after a penalty order, and the PAS-3 period for a public allotment — neither applies here.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 31 and 32 · Shelf prospectus and red herring prospectus
questions.stem: Explain the meaning of a shelf prospectus and of a red herring prospectus under the Companies Act 2013, and state the procedural requirements attaching to each. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Shelf prospectus — meaning and eligibility: a prospectus filed with the Registrar at the stage of the first offer of securities by any class or classes of companies as SEBI may provide by regulations; it must indicate a period of validity not exceeding one year commencing from the date of opening of the first offer, and no further prospectus is required for any second or subsequent offer made within that period

Shelf prospectus — information memorandum: before making a second or subsequent offer the company files an information memorandum with the Registrar, in the prescribed form and within the prescribed time, stating the new charges created, the changes in the financial position between the first offer and the succeeding offer, and other prescribed matters; the information memorandum together with the shelf prospectus constitutes the prospectus for that offer

Shelf prospectus — protection of advance applicants: where applications with advance payment have been received before a change is noted in the information memorandum, the company must intimate the changes to those applicants, and if any of them wishes to withdraw the application it must refund the whole of the money received as advance payment, within the prescribed time and manner

Red herring prospectus — meaning: a prospectus which does not include complete particulars of the quantum or price of the securities included in it; it may be issued by a company proposing to make an offer of securities prior to the issue of a prospectus
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 32(1) and the Explanation thereto

skeleton.point: Red herring prospectus — procedure: filed with the Registrar at least three days before the opening of the subscription list and the offer; it carries the same obligations as a prospectus and any variation between it and the prospectus is highlighted as variations in the prospectus; upon closing of the offer, the prospectus stating the total capital raised (whether by debt or share capital), the closing price of the securities and any other details not included in the red herring prospectus is filed with the Registrar and SEBI

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 26 · Matters to be stated and registration of a prospectus
questions.stem: State the requirements of section 26 of the Companies Act 2013 as to the matters to be stated in a prospectus, the expert's consent, and the dating, signing and registration of a prospectus. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Contents — identity and offer: every prospectus issued by or on behalf of a public company must be dated and signed and must state the name and registered-office address of the company and the names and addresses of the company secretary, chief financial officer, auditors, bankers, trustees for debenture holders and underwriters; the dates of opening and closing of the issue; a declaration about the issue of the allotment letter and refunds within the prescribed time; a Board statement that all monies received out of the issue will be transferred to a separate bank account as mentioned in section 40(3); details of monies utilised and not utilised out of previous issues; and the capital structure

Contents — the project and the risks: the main objects of the public offer and the terms of the present issue, the minimum subscription, the premium payable, the procedure and time schedule for allotment and issue of securities, the authority for the issue with the details of the resolution passed, the details of directors including appointments and remuneration, management's perception of the risk factors specific to the project, the gestation period of the project and the deadlines for completion, and any litigation or legal action pending or taken by a Government Department or a statutory body during the last five years immediately preceding the issue against the promoter

Reports: the prospectus must set out the reports for the purposes of the financial information specified in the section, including the auditor's report relating to the profits and losses and the assets and liabilities of the company and, where applicable, of its subsidiary, in the prescribed form

Expert's consent: where a prospectus includes a statement made by an expert, the expert must have given his written consent to the issue and must not have withdrawn it before the delivery of a copy of the prospectus to the Registrar, and the prospectus must state that he has given his consent and has not withdrawn it; 'expert' means a person who is not, and has not been, engaged or interested in the formation, promotion or management of the company
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 26(3) and the Explanation thereto

skeleton.point: Dating, signing, registration and validity: no prospectus may be issued unless, on or before the date of its publication, a copy signed by every person named in it as a director or proposed director (or by his duly authorised attorney) has been delivered to the Registrar for registration, with every expert's consent endorsed or attached; the prospectus must state on its face that a copy has been so delivered and specify the documents delivered; the Registrar shall not register it unless the written consents of every person named in it as auditor, legal adviser, attorney, solicitor, banker or broker accompany it; and a prospectus is NOT VALID if issued more than ninety days after the date on which a copy was delivered to the Registrar

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 34, 35 and 37 · Liability for misstatements in a prospectus
questions.stem: Distinguish between the criminal liability under section 34 and the civil liability under section 35 of the Companies Act 2013 for misstatements in a prospectus, setting out in each case who is liable and what defences are available. Also state who may take action under section 37. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 34 — criminal liability: where a prospectus issued, circulated or distributed under Chapter III includes any statement which is untrue or misleading in form or context, or where any inclusion or omission of any matter is likely to mislead, every person who authorises the issue of such prospectus is liable for action under section 447; no proof of reliance by any investor is required

Section 34 — the defence: a person is not liable if he proves that the statement or omission was immaterial, OR that he had reasonable grounds to believe, and did up to the time of the issue of the prospectus believe, that the statement was true or that the inclusion or omission was necessary

Section 35 — civil liability, who may claim and who is liable: where a person has subscribed for securities acting on a misleading statement, inclusion or omission in the prospectus and has sustained loss or damage, the company and every person who is a director at the time of the issue, who has authorised himself to be named and is named as a director or as having agreed to become a director, who is a promoter, who has authorised the issue of the prospectus, or who is an expert whose statement is included, is liable to pay compensation to every person who sustained such loss or damage — without prejudice to punishment under section 36

Section 35 — the defences: that, having consented to become a director, he withdrew his consent before the issue of the prospectus and it was issued without his authority or consent; or that the prospectus was issued without his knowledge or consent and that, on becoming aware of its issue, he forthwith gave a reasonable public notice to that effect

Section 35(3) — fraud: where it is proved that the prospectus was issued with intent to defraud the applicants or any other person, or for any fraudulent purpose, every person referred to in section 35(1) is personally responsible, WITHOUT ANY LIMITATION OF LIABILITY, for all or any of the losses or damages incurred by any person who subscribed on the basis of that prospectus

Section 37 — class action: a suit may be filed or any other action taken under section 34, section 35 or section 36 by any person, group of persons or association of persons affected by any misleading statement or by the inclusion or omission of any matter in the prospectus; the section confers standing and does not create a fresh wrong

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 39 and 40 · Allotment, minimum subscription and application money
questions.stem: Explain the conditions governing the allotment of securities offered to the public under section 39 of the Companies Act 2013, and state how the application money must be dealt with under section 40. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Minimum subscription: no allotment of any securities of a company offered to the public for subscription shall be made unless the amount stated in the prospectus as the minimum amount has been subscribed AND the sums payable on application for the amount so stated have been paid to and received by the company by cheque or other instrument

Minimum application money: the amount payable on application on every security shall not be less than five per cent of the NOMINAL amount of the security, or such other percentage or amount as may be specified by SEBI by regulations

Failure of the issue: if the stated minimum amount has not been subscribed and the sum payable on application is not received within thirty days from the date of issue of the prospectus, or such other period as may be specified by SEBI, the amount received must be returned within such time and manner as may be prescribed

Return of allotment and penalty: whenever a company having a share capital makes any allotment of securities it must file with the Registrar a return of allotment in the prescribed manner; on default under section 39(3) or 39(4) the company and its officer in default are liable to a penalty, for each default, of one thousand rupees for each day during which the default continues or one lakh rupees, whichever is less

Application money under section 40: all monies received on application from the public for subscription must be kept in a separate bank account in a scheduled bank and used only for adjustment against allotment of securities where they have been permitted to be dealt with in the stock exchange, or for repayment of monies where the company is for any other reason unable to allot securities; any condition purporting to require or bind an applicant to waive compliance with any requirement of section 40 is void

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 42 · Private placement
questions.stem: State the conditions subject to which a company may make a private placement of securities under section 42 of the Companies Act 2013, and the consequences of contravening them. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Identified persons and the cap: a private placement may be made only to a select group of persons identified by the Board, whose number shall not exceed the prescribed maximum in a financial year — presently two hundred persons in the aggregate in a financial year, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees offered securities under a scheme of employees' stock option (rules-level, amendment-sensitive)
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(2) read with r. 14, Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules 2014

skeleton.point: The offer document: the company issues a private placement offer and application in the prescribed form and manner to the identified persons, whose names and addresses are recorded by the company in the prescribed manner; the offer and application shall NOT carry any right of renunciation
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(3) and its proviso

skeleton.point: Payment, separate account and use of money: every identified person willing to subscribe applies along with the subscription money paid by cheque, demand draft or other banking channel and NOT by cash; the monies received must be kept in a separate bank account in a scheduled bank and used only for adjustment against allotment or for repayment where the company is unable to allot; and the company shall not utilise the monies raised unless allotment is made AND the return of allotment is filed with the Registrar
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(4), its proviso, and the proviso to s. 42(6)

skeleton.point: Timelines: no fresh offer or invitation may be made unless the allotments with respect to any earlier offer or invitation have been completed or that offer has been withdrawn or abandoned; the company must allot securities within sixty days from the date of receipt of the application money; failing that it must repay the application money within fifteen days from the expiry of the sixty days; and failing that it must repay with interest at twelve per cent per annum from the expiry of the sixtieth day

No publicity and the return of allotment: the company shall not release any public advertisements or utilise any media, marketing or distribution channels or agents to inform the public at large about the issue; and it must file with the Registrar a return of allotment within fifteen days from the date of allotment, including a complete list of all allottees with their full names, addresses and the number of securities allotted

Consequences of contravention: default in filing the return of allotment makes the company, its promoters and directors liable to a penalty for each default of one thousand rupees for each day of continuing default, not exceeding twenty-five lakh rupees; making an offer or accepting monies in contravention of the section makes the company, its promoters and directors liable to a penalty which may extend to the amount raised through the private placement or two crore rupees, whichever is LOWER, and the company must refund all monies with interest as specified in section 42(6) within thirty days of the order imposing the penalty; and under Explanation III an offer to more than the prescribed number of persons is deemed to be an offer to the public governed by Part I of Chapter III
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(9), s. 42(10) and Explanation III to s. 42

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 25, 28 and 27 · Deemed prospectus and variation of terms
questions.stem: Explain when a document by which securities are offered for sale to the public is deemed to be a prospectus issued by the company, and state the conditions subject to which a company may vary the terms of a contract referred to in a prospectus or the objects for which the prospectus was issued. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Deemed prospectus — the rule: where a company allots or agrees to allot securities with a view to all or any of them being offered for sale to the public, any document by which the offer for sale to the public is made is deemed to be a prospectus issued by the company, and all enactments and rules as to the contents of a prospectus and as to liability in respect of misstatements and otherwise apply as if the securities had been offered to the public directly by the company

Deemed prospectus — the presumption and the extra contents: it is evidence that the allotment was made with a view to an offer for sale to the public if either the offer for sale was made within six months after the allotment or agreement to allot, OR at the date of the offer the whole consideration to be received by the company had not been so received; the document must additionally state the net amount of the consideration received or to be received by the company and the place and time at which the allotment contract may be inspected, and it may be signed on behalf of a company by two directors or, for a firm, by not less than one-half of the partners

Offer for sale by members: where certain members of a company propose, in consultation with the Board, to offer the whole or part of their holding of shares to the public, they may do so in accordance with the prescribed procedure; any document by which the offer is made is deemed to be a prospectus issued by the company, all laws relating to a prospectus apply to it, and the members making the offer must reimburse the company all expenses incurred by it on the offer

Variation under section 27: a company shall not at any time vary the terms of a contract referred to in the prospectus, or the objects for which the prospectus was issued, except subject to the approval of, or authority given by, the company in general meeting by way of a SPECIAL RESOLUTION; the details of the notice must be published in two newspapers — one in English and one in the vernacular language of the city where the registered office is situated — and on the company's website, with the justification for the variation; the company shall not use any amount raised through the prospectus for buying, trading or otherwise dealing in equity shares of any other listed company; and dissenting shareholders must be given an exit offer by the promoters or controlling shareholders at such exit price and in such manner and conditions as may be specified by SEBI

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Case: a private placement that goes wrong
questions.case: Nilgiri Biotech Private Limited resolves to raise funds by private placement in the financial year 2026-27. Its Board identifies 120 persons and issues the private placement offer-cum-application letter to them. The company receives ₹6,00,00,000 of application money from those persons on 20 June 2026 and deposits it in a separate account with a scheduled bank. The Board then deadlocks over the valuation and makes no allotment at all; the money is finally returned to the subscribers on 19 February 2027. Separately, in the same financial year, the company offers securities to 25 qualified institutional buyers and to 40 employees under a scheme of employees' stock option. In August 2026, while the June offer is still pending and no allotment has been made or the offer withdrawn, the managing director proposes to issue a fresh private placement offer to 15 new investors and to place an advertisement describing the issue in a national business daily. Assume the prescribed maximum number of identified persons is 200, and that interest under section 42(6) is computed on a simple-interest basis for complete months.

readLink.label: Read: Private placement — s. 42 →

questions.stem: The last date by which Nilgiri Biotech was required to allot the securities was:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(6) — sixty days from the date of receipt of the application money

options.text: 18 August 2026
options.explanation: One day short. Day 1 of the sixty is 21 June, so day 60 falls on 19 August 2026.

options.text: 3 September 2026
options.explanation: This is sixty days plus a further fifteen — the outer date for REPAYMENT, not for allotment.

options.text: 18 September 2026
options.explanation: This is 90 days, which is the section 26(8) prospectus-validity period and has no application to a private placement.

options.text: 19 August 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Sixty days from 20 June 2026: 10 days take the count to 30 June, 31 more to 31 July (day 41), and 19 more to 19 August 2026.

questions.stem: Because the money was returned only on 19 February 2027, interest is payable under section 42(6). The amount of that interest is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(6) — twelve per cent per annum from the expiry of the sixtieth day

options.explanation: Correct. Interest runs from the expiry of the sixtieth day, that is from 19 August 2026, to the date of repayment on 19 February 2027 — six complete months. ₹6,00,00,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹36,00,000.
This charges a full year's interest. The default period is six months, not twelve.
This applies six per cent per annum. Section 42(6) fixes the rate at twelve per cent per annum.
This runs the interest from 19 September 2026, giving five months. The section starts the clock at the expiry of the SIXTIETH day — 19 August 2026 — not later.

questions.stem: On the managing director's two August proposals — a fresh private placement offer to 15 new investors, and an advertisement in a national business daily — the correct position is:

options.text: Both are permissible, since the 15 new investors are well within the cap of 200 identified persons and an advertisement merely informs the market
options.explanation: The cap is not the only constraint. Section 42(5) bars the fresh offer and s. 42(7) bars the advertisement outright.

options.text: The fresh offer is permissible but the advertisement is not, provided the fresh offer is made only to persons already identified by the Board
options.explanation: The fresh offer is barred whoever it is made to, because the earlier offer is neither completed nor withdrawn.

options.text: Neither is permissible: no fresh offer may be made while allotments on an earlier offer are incomplete and that offer has not been withdrawn or abandoned, and no public advertisement or media, marketing or distribution channel or agent may be used to inform the public at large about the issue
options.explanation: Correct. Section 42(5) prohibits a fresh offer until the earlier one is completed, withdrawn or abandoned; s. 42(7) prohibits public advertisements and the use of media, marketing or distribution channels or agents. A private placement that is advertised is a contradiction in terms.

options.text: Both are permissible if the company first files a return of allotment for the June offer with the Registrar
options.explanation: No allotment was made, so no return of allotment can be filed; and filing a return would not lift the s. 42(7) advertising ban in any event.

questions.stem: Ignoring the June offer's fate, the number of FURTHER identified persons to whom Nilgiri Biotech may offer securities by private placement in the financial year 2026-27 is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 42(2) read with r. 14, Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules 2014 (rules-level)

options.explanation: This counts the 25 qualified institutional buyers against the cap. QIBs are expressly excluded from the count.
Correct. 200 − 120 = 80. Qualified institutional buyers and employees offered securities under an ESOP scheme do not consume the cap, so neither the 25 nor the 40 reduces the headroom.
This counts the 40 ESOP employees against the cap. They are expressly excluded.
This counts both the qualified institutional buyers and the ESOP employees against the cap; both exclusions have been ignored.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Case: misstatement in a prospectus
questions.case: Sabarmati Green Energy Limited makes a public offer through a prospectus which materially overstates its confirmed order book. P, a director at the time of the issue, chaired the meeting that approved the prospectus and knew that the largest order in it had been cancelled. Q had agreed in writing in March 2026 to become a director and was named in the prospectus as having agreed to become a director; she withdrew her consent in writing on 2 April 2026, and the prospectus was issued on 20 April 2026 without her authority or consent. R is an independent valuer whose report, given with his written consent under section 26(3), contains the overstated order-book figure. W read the prospectus, subscribed for 40,000 shares in reliance on the order-book statement, and suffered loss when the true position emerged. Separately, V, who is unconnected with the company, applied fourteen times in different combinations of his name and surname and was allotted shares in each application, making a gain on their sale. Some 300 investors who subscribed on the strength of the prospectus now wish to proceed jointly.

readLink.label: Read: Civil liability for misstatements — s. 35 →

questions.stem: As regards P, the correct position is:

options.text: He is liable under section 34 for action under section 447, having authorised the issue of a prospectus containing an untrue statement with no belief in its truth, and he is additionally liable under section 35(1)(a) to compensate W; if fraudulent intent is proved, section 35(3) makes him personally responsible without any limitation of liability
options.explanation: Correct. Section 34 catches every person who authorises the issue, and the proviso is unavailable because P neither believed the statement nor can call it immaterial. Section 35(1)(a) makes a director at the time of the issue liable to compensate a subscriber who acted on the statement and suffered loss, and s. 35(3) removes the ceiling where fraudulent intent is proved.

options.text: He is liable only to compensate W under section 35, criminal liability under section 34 being confined to the company
options.explanation: Section 34 fastens on persons who authorise the issue, not on the company as such.

options.text: He escapes liability under section 34 because he did not personally draft the order-book statement
options.explanation: The proviso to s. 34 turns on materiality and belief, not on authorship.

options.text: He is liable under section 38, since he induced the company to allot securities
options.explanation: Section 38 punishes an applicant who uses a fictitious name or multiple applications. It has no application to a director who authorises a misleading prospectus.

questions.stem: As regards Q, the correct position is:

options.text: She is liable, because she is named in the prospectus as having agreed to become a director and liability under section 35(1)(b) is absolute
options.explanation: Section 35(1)(b) would catch her, but s. 35(2) supplies the defence, and on these facts it is made out.

options.text: She is liable, but only to the extent of the amount she would have received as director's remuneration
options.explanation: Section 35 contains no such measure of liability; and in any event she has a complete defence.

options.text: She is not liable, because having consented to become a director she withdrew her consent before the issue of the prospectus, and it was issued without her authority or consent
options.explanation: Correct. This is s. 35(2)(a) exactly: consent withdrawn before the issue, and the prospectus issued without her authority or consent. Had she merely disagreed without withdrawing, limb (b) of s. 35(1) would have caught her.

options.text: She is not liable, because a person who has not actually been appointed a director can never fall within section 35(1)
options.explanation: Section 35(1)(b) expressly reaches a person named as having agreed to become a director, immediately or after an interval of time. Her escape is the s. 35(2)(a) defence, not the absence of appointment.

questions.stem: As regards V, the correct position is:

options.text: He commits no offence, because each application was made in a variation of his own real name and no fictitious person was involved
options.explanation: Section 38(1)(b) expressly catches multiple applications 'in different names or in different combinations of his name or surname'. Using his own name in combinations is the offence.

options.text: He is liable for action under section 447 for making multiple applications in different combinations of his name or surname, and on conviction the Court may also order disgorgement of his gain and the seizure and disposal of the securities in his possession, the amount received being credited to the Investor Education and Protection Fund
options.explanation: Correct. Section 38(1)(b) applies, s. 38(3) supplies the disgorgement and seizure powers, and s. 38(4) sends the proceeds to the Investor Education and Protection Fund. Note that section 38(1) must also be reproduced prominently in every prospectus and application form under s. 38(2).

options.text: He is liable under section 36, since he induced the company to allot securities to him
