options.explanation: Section 36 concerns false statements, promises or forecasts made to induce another person to invest or to obtain credit. Section 38 is the provision aimed at the applicant who applies multiply or in a fictitious name.

options.text: His only exposure is that the company may cancel the allotments and refund his money
options.explanation: That understates the position considerably: s. 38 attracts action under s. 447 and the loss of both the gain and the securities.

questions.stem: The 300 investors who subscribed on the strength of the prospectus and wish to proceed jointly:

options.text: Must each file a separate suit, since the Companies Act 2013 makes no provision for joint action on a misleading prospectus
options.explanation: Section 37 exists precisely to avoid that result.

options.text: May proceed jointly only if they collectively hold at least ten per cent of the issued share capital of the company
options.explanation: A shareholding threshold governs the separate class-action remedy under s. 245; s. 37 imposes no such threshold for prospectus misstatements.

options.text: May proceed jointly only against the company, and not against its directors, promoters or experts
options.explanation: Section 37 permits action under ss. 34, 35 and 36, which reach individuals as well as the company.

options.text: May file a suit or take any other action under section 34, section 35 or section 36 as a group of persons affected by the misleading statement in the prospectus
options.explanation: Correct. Section 37 confers standing on any person, group of persons or association of persons affected by a misleading statement or by the inclusion or omission of any matter in the prospectus. It creates no new wrong — it opens the door to the existing ones.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Case: a public offer, registration and application money
questions.case: Vaigai Textiles Limited, a public company, proposes a public offer of 12,00,000 equity shares of ₹100 each at ₹250 per share. A copy of the prospectus signed by every person named in it as a director was delivered to the Registrar for registration on 12 May 2026, and the Registrar registered it on 19 May 2026. Waiting for better market conditions, the company published the prospectus and opened the subscription list on 20 August 2026. Application money received from the public was credited to the company's ordinary current account, and ₹40,00,000 of it was used to pay a trade supplier before any allotment was made. By the end of the thirtieth day from the issue of the prospectus, the minimum amount stated in the prospectus had not been subscribed. SEBI has specified no percentage or period other than those in the Act.

readLink.label: Read: Matters to be stated and registration — s. 26 →

questions.stem: On the validity of the prospectus published on 20 August 2026, the correct position is:

options.text: It is valid, because the ninety days run from the date on which the Registrar registered the prospectus, namely 19 May 2026
options.explanation: The clock is fixed to delivery, not to registration. This is the most attractive wrong answer because it gains the company a week.

options.text: It is not valid, because it was issued more than ninety days after 12 May 2026, the date on which a copy was delivered to the Registrar for registration
options.explanation: Correct. Ninety days from 12 May 2026 expired on 10 August 2026, so the publication on 20 August 2026 was ten days out of time. Under s. 26(8) the prospectus is not valid, and a fresh copy must be delivered.

options.text: It is valid, because section 26(8) applies only where the prospectus has not been registered at all
options.explanation: Section 26(8) applies to a registered prospectus; it is a shelf-life rule, not a registration rule.

options.text: It is valid, because the ninety-day period may be extended by the Registrar on the company's application
options.explanation: Section 26(8) gives the Registrar no power of extension.

questions.stem: The minimum amount payable on application on the whole issue, calculated under section 39(2), is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 39(2) — five per cent of the nominal amount of the security

options.explanation: Correct. The floor is five per cent of the NOMINAL amount: 5% × ₹100 = ₹5 per share, and ₹5 × 12,00,000 shares = ₹60,00,000. The issue price of ₹250 is irrelevant to this computation.
This applies five per cent to the issue price of ₹250. Section 39(2) uses the nominal amount as the base — unlike the underwriting-commission cap under section 40(6), which uses the issue price.
This applies 2.5% to the nominal amount — the debenture commission rate, imported into the wrong provision.
This applies ten per cent to the nominal amount. The statutory floor is five per cent.

questions.stem: On the treatment of the application money received from the public, the correct position is:

options.text: There is no contravention, because the money belonged to the company from the moment it was received
options.explanation: Section 40(3) exists precisely to deny that. Until allotment, the money is held for a restricted purpose.

options.text: There is no contravention, provided the company discloses the use of the money in its next annual report
options.explanation: Later disclosure does not cure a breach of s. 40(3).

options.text: There is a contravention only in respect of the ₹40,00,000 actually spent, the crediting of the money to the current account being immaterial
options.explanation: Both steps breach the section: s. 40(3) requires a separate bank account in a scheduled bank as well as restricting the use of the money.

options.text: There is a contravention: all monies received on application must be kept in a separate bank account in a scheduled bank and may be used only for adjustment against allotment where the securities have been permitted to be dealt with in a stock exchange, or for repayment where the company is unable to allot; any clause binding an applicant to waive that requirement would also be void
options.explanation: Correct. Crediting the money to the ordinary current account breaches the separate-account requirement, and paying a trade supplier is outside the two permitted uses in s. 40(3)(a) and (b). Section 40(4) adds that no waiver clause can save the company.

questions.stem: The minimum amount stated in the prospectus not having been subscribed within thirty days from the date of issue of the prospectus, the company must:

options.text: Allot the securities to the extent subscribed and carry the shortfall to the next issue
options.explanation: Section 39(1) prohibits any allotment at all until the minimum amount is subscribed and received.

options.text: Apply to the Registrar for permission to allot the securities notwithstanding the shortfall
options.explanation: The Registrar has no dispensing power under s. 39.

options.text: Make no allotment and return the amount received within such time and manner as may be prescribed, failing which the company and its officer in default are liable to a penalty, for each default, of ₹1,000 for each day of continuing default or ₹1,00,000, whichever is less
options.explanation: Correct. Section 39(1) bars allotment, s. 39(3) requires the money to be returned as prescribed, and s. 39(5) fixes the penalty at ₹1,000 per day of continuing default or ₹1,00,000, whichever is LESS, for each default, on the company and on the officer in default.

options.text: Make no allotment, and forfeit the application money to the Investor Education and Protection Fund
options.explanation: The money goes back to the applicants. The Investor Education and Protection Fund receives disgorged amounts under s. 38(4) and unclaimed sums, not a failed issue's application money.
